title: Let no one say it truly
hookLine: let no one be able to say truly that you aren't simple or good (Meditations 10.32)

lines: LET NO ONE SAY IT TRULY.
cards: Someone says something about you behind your back. Selfish, they say, or fake, or lazy. It stings, and soon you're arguing with them in your head, in the shower, on the drive.
But there's a quieter question under the sting: is it true? Marcus doesn't tell himself to stop people talking. He tells himself something harder, and much more in his control.

teach.h: LET THEM BE WRONG ABOUT YOU.
teach.b: First, the line. Let no one be able to say truthfully of you, Marcus writes, that you are not simple, or not good. Let anyone who thinks that of you be a liar.
Second, the shift. He isn't trying to control what people say. People will say what they say.
He's trying to control whether it's true.
You can't stop the rumor. You can make it false. Third, it's in your power.
All of this, he writes, is up to you.

teach.h: WHO CAN STOP YOU BEING GOOD?
teach.b: Who can stop you from being good and simple? No one. Others can mislabel you, but they can't make the label stick to the person you actually are.
Fourth, the test. When a remark lands, there are two questions. Is it true?
If it isn't, it's their mistake, and you can let it go.
If it is, even a little, you've been handed a free piece of information, and the work is to make it false.

Either way, the energy goes into living, not defending. And notice his pair of words: simple and good, the same pair book ten opened with, when he asked his soul whether it would ever be good and simple.
A few pages later, he's still working on it.

how: People who use this passage often answer criticism by first asking whether it's true, and if any part is, by quietly changing that part rather than arguing.

o: two ways to prove a critic wrong in front of everyone
a pair of checks to run before you answer back to a critic
Marcus's test: is it true, and if so, how to make it false

games.q: let no one say it truly — tap the pairs.
p: what Marcus wants no one to deny

s: Marcus tells himself to make people stop criticizing him
he aims to make the criticism false, not to silence it.
he says being simple and good is in your own power
who can stop you from being good and simple? he asks.

games.q: you hear that someone called you fake. you're Marcus. what do you do?
o: confront them and demand they take it back.
ask whether it's true, and live so that it isn't.
games.why: let no one be able to say truly that you aren't simple or good, he writes; let whoever thinks it be a liar. that part is in your power.

practice: Bring to mind one criticism you've heard about yourself, or one you're afraid of, and ask gently whether there's any truth in it. If there's none, set it down.
If there's some, picture the one act that would make it false: the generous thing for selfish, the plain thing for fake, the finished thing for lazy.

wordCard.voice: Two questions. Marcus's test for criticism: is it true, and if so, what will you do to make it false. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: truly, truthfully. Marcus wants no one to be able to name his faults alēthōs.

carryVoice: Your line: let it be false. You can't stop the rumor, but you can make it untrue. See you tomorrow.
